Material Principle (of the Reformation)
muh-TEER-ee-uhl PRIN-suh-puhl
n. phrase (Reformation theology)
From Latin principium materiale: materia (matter, content, substance) + principium (first principle, ruling norm). Where the formal principle answers the question of authority, the material principle answers the question of content. The Reformers identified justification by grace alone through faith alone as the central doctrinal substance of the gospel they had recovered from medieval obscurity.

Biblical Definition

The material principle of the Reformation is justification by faith alone (sola fide)—the doctrine Luther called the articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae (the article by which the church stands or falls). It answers: What is the central saving truth that Scripture proclaims? Paul's letter to the Romans declares it: “For in it the righteousness of God is revealed—from faith to faith. As it is written: 'But the righteous man shall live by faith'” (Rom 1:17). Habakkuk saw it in the exile: “the righteous will live by his faith” (Hab 2:4). Paul argues it against the Judaizers: “Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.” (Gal 2:16). And the Ephesian letter places it in the architecture of grace: “For by grace you have been saved through faith—and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8). The material principle does not stand alone but depends on the formal principle: it is Scripture's authority that requires justification by faith to be believed; it is Scripture's clarity that makes the doctrine knowable. Together, the formal and material principles form the Reformation's intellectual backbone. Where the formal principle identifies how we know (by Scripture), the material principle identifies what we must know to be saved (that we are justified by Christ's righteousness received through faith alone). The 1689 London Baptist Confession (11.1–3) expounds the material principle as the heart of the gospel.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Reformation's central saving doctrine—justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone—the substance and heartbeat of the gospel that the Reformers recovered from medieval theological corruption.

MATERIAL PRINCIPLE, n. phrase. In Reformation and Reformed scholastic theology, the central doctrinal content of the gospel—justification by faith alone (sola fide)—the article Luther declared the church stands or falls by.

Contrasted with formal principle: the formal principle determines the court of appeal (Scripture alone); the material principle is the central truth that court of appeal reveals (the sinner is justified by God's grace, through faith, on the basis of Christ's imputed righteousness alone).

Luther's rediscovery of the material principle came through his Turmerlebnis (tower experience), c. 1515: meditating on Rom 1:17, he saw that the “righteousness of God” Paul speaks of is not the righteousness God demands from us but the righteousness He gives to us through faith in Christ. This overturned the entire medieval penitential structure.

The material principle is not the whole of Christian doctrine but it is the centrum: every other doctrine either supports, flows from, or must be consistent with justification by faith alone. Where the material principle is denied or diluted, the gospel is lost.

Rome's formal denial at Trent (1547, canon 9): “If anyone says that by faith alone the impious is justified...let him be anathema.” The anathema still stands; the Reformation reply is that Scripture still says otherwise.

Key Scripture

Romans 1:17 — "For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith."

Habakkuk 2:4 — "Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith."

Galatians 2:16 — "Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified."

Ephesians 2:8 — "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:"

Modern Corruption

Rome added works, merit, and sacramental cooperation to justification (Trent, 1547). Modern evangelicalism softens the material principle by blending faith with ongoing moral performance, progressive sanctification as a condition of justification, or therapeutic self-improvement as the goal of the gospel.

expand to see more

The Roman Catholic Council of Trent (1547) formally condemned the material principle: Canon 9 declared that anyone who says the sinner is justified by faith alone, without works, is anathema. Trent taught that justification is a process of moral renovation infused into the soul through the sacraments, that merit accrues through penance and indulgences, and that final salvation depends on the cooperation of human will with divine grace. This is not a different emphasis on the same doctrine; it is a different doctrine. Luther called it another gospel (Gal 1:8–9). The 1689 LBCF (11.2) insists that faith justifies solely as the instrument of receiving Christ's imputed righteousness, not as itself a work.

The evangelical corruption is less open but equally corrosive. When preaching frames the gospel as God's help for moral improvement, when assurance is conditioned on progressive sanctification levels, when “accepting Christ” means joining a community of changed people rather than receiving the alien righteousness of Another, the material principle has been hollowed out. The Reformers' word for this is “works-righteousness”—not salvation by outright wickedness but salvation by human contribution, however modest. The material principle tolerates no contribution: the righteousness that justifies is “not of yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin scholastic principium materiale, applied by the Reformers to identify justification by faith alone as the central saving content of the gospel Scripture proclaims.

expand to see more

Latin materia — matter, substance, content; the material principle is the substantive truth at the heart of the Reformation's doctrinal recovery.

Latin articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae — the article by which the church stands or falls; Luther's phrase identifying justification as the hinge on which everything else turns.

Hebrew emunatho (Hab 2:4) — his faith/faithfulness; Paul quotes this verse in both Romans and Galatians as the OT foundation for justification by faith.

Greek dikaioô — to justify, to declare righteous; a forensic verdict, not a moral renovation—the imputation of Christ's righteousness to the believing sinner's account.

Sola fide — faith alone; the Reformation's formulation of the material principle, insisting that faith is the sole instrument (never the merit) of justification.

Usage

"The material principle is the heart of the gospel: the sinner stands before God justified—declared righteous—not because of anything done or felt or cooperated with, but because Christ's righteousness has been credited to their account through faith."

"When the material principle is lost, the church becomes a moral-improvement society; when it is recovered, the church becomes a community of sinners forgiven and freed by God's grace."

"The formal and material principles cannot be separated: the authority of Scripture (formal) establishes that justification by faith (material) is God's own declared way of salvation—not a tradition, not a preference, but the revealed gospel."
